Asking how deep the branching hierarchy goes means order_from_tip. Asking how balanced it is means strahler_order. The one thing not to do is compare numbers across schemes.

order_res$summary
#>   order n_segments n_tips n_branch_points total_length cumulative_length
#> 1     1         26      6              22   5.16391097          5.163911
#> 2     2         38     25              13   3.30586934          8.469780
#> 3     3         27     15              14   4.75573400         13.225514
#> 4     4         14     12               2   0.71618856         13.941703
#> 5     5          4      2               2   1.91089531         15.852598
#> 6     6          2      2               0   0.04935045         15.901949
#>   cumulative_fraction mean_segment_length branching_frequency mean_diameter
#> 1           0.3247345          0.19861196            4.260337    0.06893584
#> 2           0.5326253          0.08699656            3.932400    0.04545475
#> 3           0.8316914          0.17613830            2.943815    0.06355430
#> 4           0.8767292          0.05115633            2.792561    0.04367593
#> 5           0.9968966          0.47772383            1.046630    0.04563837
#> 6           1.0000000          0.02467522            0.000000    0.03223201
#>   median_diameter
#> 1      0.06845654
#> 2      0.04095795
#> 3      0.04190786
#> 4      0.03722479
#> 5      0.03825043
#> 6      0.03160465

# The thickest order class against everything else, picked by diameter rather
# than by order number, so the same call means the same thing across a dataset.
order_metrics(order_res, groups = "thickest")
#>      group    orders n_segments n_tips n_branch_points total_length
#> 1 thickest         1         26      6              22     5.163911
#> 2     rest 2,3,4,5,6         85     56              31    10.738038
#>   length_fraction mean_segment_length branching_frequency mean_diameter
#> 1       0.3247345           0.1986120            4.260337    0.06893584
#> 2       0.6752655           0.1263299            2.886933    0.05332406
#>   median_diameter
#> 1      0.06845654
#> 2      0.03993719

Tips and branch points come from this table too: n_tips and n_branch_points per segment, summed per order class in $summary.

diam_fb   <- root_diameter(fb_clean, skeleton_img = fb_skl_pruned,
                           unit = "cm", dpi = 1200, select_layer = NULL)
diam_vals <- diam_fb$diameters      # the per-skeleton-pixel values

cat(sprintf("diameter mean %.4f cm | sd %.4f | max %.4f cm\n",
            mean(diam_vals), stats::sd(diam_vals), max(diam_vals)))
#> diameter mean 0.0618 cm | sd 0.0164 | max 0.1108 cm

ggplot(data.frame(diameter = diam_vals), aes(x = diameter)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 24, fill = "steelblue4", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Diameter (cm)", y = "Count",
       title = "Root diameter distribution")

A diameter distribution is where fine and coarse roots separate, and modal_peaks() finds the modes in it, optionally refining them with a Gaussian mixture via mclust. It is not run here because this one distribution is unimodal: a single peak with a long upper tail, which is what a scan of mostly fine roots looks like. Run it where the histogram shows two humps and you want the cut between them placed by the data rather than by eye.

Network shape and transport

Two questions the segment table answers once it exists, both working on order_res$edges rather than on the image.

net <- network_metrics(order_res$edges, topology = "projected_tree")
net$traits
#> $n_nodes
#> [1] 115
#> 
#> $n_edges
#> [1] 111
#> 
#> $n_components
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $n_tips
#> [1] 62
#> 
#> $n_branch_points
#> [1] 53
#> 
#> $tip_ratio
#> [1] 0.5391304
#> 
#> $beta
#> [1] 0.9652174
#> 
#> $total_length
#> [1] 15.90195
#> 
#> $mean_edge_length
#> [1] 0.1432608
net$qc
#> $cyclomatic
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $alpha_meshedness
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $gamma
#> [1] 0.3274336
#> 
#> $n_self_loops
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $n_duplicate_edges
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $is_forest
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $artefact_cycles
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $artefact_rate
#> [1] 0
net$note
#> [1] "loops in a projected tree are crossings the segmentation did not separate; artefact_rate divides that count by network length, in whatever unit the edge table carries, so images can be compared"

$traits is the shape of the network: node and edge counts, how many separate pieces, how many tips, the tip ratio, and beta – edges per node, which is the plainest measure of how branchy a network is. $qc holds the loop arithmetic. The same numbers land in one place or the other depending on the topology you declare, and nothing else changes:

topology What a loop means Where loop counts go
"tree" impossible $qc: any loop means the input is not a tree
"projected_tree" crossings in projection $qc: unresolved overlaps
"reticulate" real, e.g. mycelium $traits: a measurement

On a root scan a closed circuit is almost never one the plant grew; it is two roots crossing in front of one another, touching in the image, joined by the skeleton. So artefact_cycles counts them and artefact_rate divides by total network length, which makes the count comparable between a large root system and a small one. Reporting that as biology is the mistake the argument exists to prevent – which is also why "reticulate" is there: for mycelium with anastomoses, leaf venation or a stream network, the loops are the structure, and cyclomatic and alpha_meshedness move into $traits.

et <- root_transport(order_res$edges)
head(et[, c("length", "path_length", "path_resistance",
            "downstream_tips", "downstream_length")], 4)
#>       length path_length path_resistance downstream_tips downstream_length
#> 1 0.04264472    2.221137         6827712               1        0.04264472
#> 2 0.04009685    2.218590         6929970               1        0.04009685
#> 3 0.18486079    2.178493         6337904               2        0.26760236
#> 4 0.04135668    2.034989         6777683               1        0.04135668

Everything here answers one question: which parts of this root system are remote, and remote in what sense. Geometric distance from the base is one answer and hydraulic cost is another, and they disagree, because a root’s resistance scales with the fourth power of its radius. A tip at the end of a long thick root can be hydraulically closer to the base than one at the end of a short thin root. That is the comparison the figure below draws, and it is why both columns are reported.

Two families of column, and the direction of each is fixed by the base rather than by any order scheme. root_transport() picks the thickest loose end of each separate piece as the base — on a scan that is the proximal end — and everything is measured relative to that. path_length and path_resistance accumulate inward to outward: from the base to the far end of this segment, so they grow toward the tips and answer “how far is this, from the plant’s point of view”. downstream_tips, downstream_length and downstream_surface accumulate outward to inward: what lies beyond this segment, so they peak at the base and answer “how much does this segment serve”. Neither changes if you switch order = in branch_order_map(); both change if the base is picked wrongly, which is what a stray non-root object touching the mask does. Resistance is the Hagen-Poiseuille term for an open pipe, so it scales with the fourth power of radius: halving a root’s diameter makes the same length roughly sixteen times harder to push water through. Real resistance is set by xylem anatomy, not by the outer diameter, so treat these as a relative ranking within one scan rather than a physical measurement.

render_order_overlay() paints any per-segment column back onto the mask, which is how a transport quantity becomes legible. It picks its own legend: a handful of small integers gets one labeled swatch per class, anything continuous gets a color ramp with a scale bar.

png_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")

# max_side caps the longest side of the written PNG, and anything below the
# scan's own width throws pixels away: thin roots drop out rather than getting
# thicker. Keep it at the full width and zoom afterwards instead.
# A handful of thin distal segments carry resistance far above the rest, and a
# ramp stretched to that maximum leaves every other segment in nearly the same
# color. Capping the value at the 97th percentile spends the ramp on the range
# the roots actually occupy; the capped segments sit at the top color. The
# alternative is to paint log10(path_resistance) and label the bar as a log
# scale, which keeps the extremes distinguishable but makes the bar harder to
# read as a physical quantity.
cap <- stats::quantile(et$path_resistance, 0.97, na.rm = TRUE)

render_order_overlay(attr(et, "segments"),
                     pmin(et$path_resistance, cap),
                     attr(et, "dims"), png_file,
                     mask = fb_clean, max_side = 2000,
                     value_label = "path resistance (capped at p97)")

zoom_plot(as_rgb_rast(png_file), frac = fb_frac, center = fb_ctr,
          maxcell = Inf, overview = FALSE, main = "Path resistance")

Segments with no value are drawn in red, which makes failures visible rather than silently absent – a loop in the graph has no single “beyond”, so its transport columns are NA and it shows up in that color. A lot of red is the same signal network_metrics() reports as artefact_cycles.

Path length and path resistance rank the segments differently, and the reason is the radius term.

op     <- graphics::par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
pt_bg  <- grDevices::rgb(0.21, 0.35, 0.47, 0.45)
pt_cex <- 0.4 + 2.4 * et$mean_diameter / max(et$mean_diameter, na.rm = TRUE)

plot(et$path_length, et$path_resistance,
     pch = 21, bg = pt_bg, col = "steelblue4", cex = pt_cex,
     xlab = "path length from the base (cm)",
     ylab = "path resistance (relative)",
     main = "linear resistance axis")

plot(et$path_length, et$path_resistance, log = "y",
     pch = 21, bg = pt_bg, col = "steelblue4", cex = pt_cex,
     xlab = "path length from the base (cm)",
     ylab = "path resistance (relative, log)",
     main = "log resistance axis")

graphics::par(op)

The pair is worth seeing, and which one to use depends on the scan. On the linear axis a few thin segments set the top of the range and everything else is squeezed into a band along the bottom, which says only that most segments are cheap and one or two are not. The log axis spreads the same points over the orders of magnitude they actually span, and the structure appears: at any given distance from the base, resistance varies by two or three orders of magnitude. A clean scan with no stray object can be readable on the linear axis; one where a single artifact has created an extremely thin segment never is, because that segment alone sets the scale. Removing the artifact is the better fix, and the log axis is what to reach for when you cannot.

Point size is diameter, and the small points – the thin roots – sit at the top. So a long thick root can be an easier path for water than a short thin one, which is why both columns are reported rather than one standing in for the other.

Reference

What you can measure

One row per quantity, with the unit it comes back in and what it says. Lengths, diameters and depths follow unit and dpi; the table assumes "cm".

Per image, or per depth interval

Quantity Unit Meaning
rootpx, voidpx pixels root and background pixel counts
rootpx.density % root pixels as a share of the interval
rootlength cm skeleton length, Kimura estimator
rootlength.density cm cm^-2 length per unit of imaged wall
avg.diameter, max.diameter cm from 2x the distance transform
var.diameter cm^2 spread of diameter within the interval
root.surface.area cm^2 lateral area of the root cylinder
root.volume cm^3 volume of the same cylinder
n.diameter.peaks count modes in the diameter distribution
rcc, gcc, bcc fraction chromatic coordinates, sum to 1
hue, saturation 0-1 HSV of the mean color
luminosity 0-255 Rec. 709 weighted mean

Per tube or scan

Quantity Unit Meaning
mrd cm mean rooting depth, amount-weighted
total.length.density cm cm^-2 summed over the profile
rootlength.fraction fraction share of total length in an interval
deep_drive 0-1 share of root pixels heading deepest
mean.steepness.angle degrees 0 horizontal, 90 vertical
Wasserstein distance cm depth the mass must travel between profiles
Jensen-Shannon, KL nats bin-by-bin divergence, no depth metric
amplitude, offset trait units circumferential sine fit
peakTime slice index where that sine peaks around the tube

Per segment, from the branching graph

Quantity Unit Meaning
length cm along the pixel chain, junction stub included
mean_diameter cm length-weighted within the segment
order_from_tip, strahler_order count inward from the tips, per segment
order_from_base count generations outward, per root
root_max_order_from_tip count the root’s largest tip order
n_tips, n_branch_points count degree-1 and degree-3+ nodes
branching_frequency cm^-1 branch points per unit length
path_length cm base of the root system to this segment
path_resistance relative 8 eta L / (pi r^4), eta = 1
downstream_length cm root length beyond this segment
downstream_tips count tips beyond it
downstream_surface cm^2 root surface beyond it

Per network

Quantity Unit Meaning
n_nodes, n_edges count graph size
n_components count separate root systems in the image
tip_ratio fraction tips over nodes
beta edges/node how branchy the network is
cyclomatic count independent closed circuits
alpha_meshedness 0-1 loops against the planar maximum
artefact_cycles count the same, read as unresolved crossings
artefact_rate cm^-1 crossings per unit length, comparable

Conventions

Four things are read the same way everywhere, and they are the ones to check before trusting a number.

  • Pixels to physical: cm = px * 2.54 / dpi. Every function that reports a length needs dpi, and root_diameter() defaults to 300 rather than erroring.
  • Angles: angle_from_vertical and insertion_angles are degrees from vertical, [0, 90], 0 upright. mean.steepness.angle is degrees from horizontal. They are not the same convention.
  • Axes: depth runs along the image width, the tube circumference down the height. A scan with the soil surface at the top has to be turned a quarter turn first.
  • Depth zero: start_soil and soil_starts are centimeters, subtracted from every depth. estimate_soil_surface() reports pixels, so convert.

Two more are easy to misread. Diameter in the order summaries is length-weighted, so mean_diameter describes the diameter of the root length rather than the average of segment values. And the Kimura length estimators are not additive, so depth intervals do not sum to the whole-image value.

Packages this builds on

Rootopia is mostly glue and geometry. The numerical work is done by other packages, and knowing which one is behind a function tells you where to look when a result surprises you.

Package What Rootopia uses it for Required?
terra every raster: reading, extents, zonal(), plotting yes
imager connected components, morphology, the distance transform behind root_diameter() yes
transport wasserstein1d(), the earth-mover distance in compare_depth_distribution() yes
minpack.lm Levenberg-Marquardt fit in fit_sine_curve() / rhythmicity() yes
mclust Gaussian mixture clustering in modal_peaks() yes
glcm the texture matrices in analyze_soil_texture() yes
imagefx phase and cross correlation in estimate_rotation_shift() yes
raster the object type glcm and RStoolbox expect yes
dplyr, tidyr, stringr shaping the per-interval tables the wrappers return yes
landscapemetrics every metric in root_scape_metrics() suggested
RStoolbox unsupervised classification in estimate_soil_surface() and estimate_rotation_center() suggested
png, tiff reading and writing those formats in stitching and overlays suggested
ggplot2 figures in the vignettes only suggested

A suggested package is not installed with Rootopia. The functions that need one check for it and stop with a message naming it rather than failing further in, so a thin install still runs the depth-profile workflow in Part I.

The method for rhythmicity() is not original here either: it reproduces the likelihood-based rhythmicity tests of diffCircadian (Ding et al. 2021) for a spatial axis instead of a temporal one.

Availability

Rootopia is an R package, available from https://github.com/jcunow/Rootopia and not yet on CRAN. It requires R >= 4.1 for the native pipe and terra >= 1.8. help(package = "Rootopia") lists every exported function with its arguments and return value, and further worked examples ship with the package.
